units: the writer sends his message right after a training session
he used to believe the two sports called for the same abilities
both call for holding a steady pace
the burning breath of the first minutes turns up in both
when running, the joints take the shock against the ground
when swimming, the sense of weight fades away
the runner fights the slope of the ground
the swimmer fights the drag of the water
trading one for the other eased the writer's joint aches
the writer urges his reader to give it a try
text: I am writing this with my breath still ragged, straight off the session, because something clicked out there and I wanted you to hear it first. For season after season I was convinced that running and swimming asked exactly the same things of a body. They do overlap in one place: both of them want a steady pace held from start to finish, and both set your lungs burning through the opening minutes. What caught me off guard was everything else. On the road, every stride slams into the ground and my joints swallow the shock of it. In the water my weight seems to go somewhere else entirely, and all that is left is the pull of the shoulders. A runner fights the slope of a hill. A swimmer fights the water pushing back. Since I started trading one for the other, my knees have quit aching. Give it a try, then tell me how it feels.

units: the text answers the questions beginners ask most often
the warm-up should work the ankle and the hip
costly shoes are not needed
a gripping sole guards against slipping on wet ground
the early shortness of breath clears up on its own
a sharp pain signals damaged tissue
muscle repair happens during rest
outings should be lengthened in small weekly steps
the pace chosen must still allow talking
text: So you want to move more without wrecking a knee. The same handful of questions reaches me every single week, so here they are, answered in order. Warm up or not? Warm up, and not with a lazy shake of the legs, because the ankle and the hip both need waking up before you push off. Do you need costly shoes? No, you really do not. What you do need is a sole that grips, since one slide on wet ground will cost you weeks. Should it hurt? No. The gasping at the start settles by itself, but a sharp stab is tissue telling you something has torn. Train every single day? Bad idea. Muscle rebuilds itself while you rest, not while you sweat. And how do you actually get better? Stretch each outing by a handful of strides a week, hold a pace that still lets you talk, and write down how you felt.

units: the coach breaks the race into three stretches
the favorite went out far too fast
the chasing pack let her go without responding
the turn came on the steep climb of the second lap
the coach's runner passed her rivals one by one
the chaser crossed the top of the climb in front
she opened a lead on the downhill part
she accepted a slide through a muddy bend the others refused
she dropped her last rival on the closing stretch
the coach credits the win to composure rather than power
text: Caught at the finish line, the coach splits the race into three stretches. Off the line, she says, the favorite went out far too fast, and the pack behind her simply watched her go without lifting a finger. Then came the steep climb on the second lap, and the whole thing turned over. “I watched my runner pick them off one by one, and right then I knew she was going to close that gap,” she says. Her own runner crested the top of the climb in front, then stretched her lead on the way down, where the rest of them braked out of caution. “She took the slide through that muddy bend. The others refused it,” the coach adds. On the closing straight, with the crowd roaring her in, the young athlete pulled clear of her last rival. “Power did not win that race. A cool head did,” she says, her voice catching.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: running was at first a duty tied to survival
it served to chase game, to carry word, or to escape a threat
the reliance on endurance favored legs able to hold a pace for long
that pressure shaped a springy tendon at the heel
it also produced heavy sweating
a ligament holds the neck steady during the stride
the spread of settlements and pack animals cut that need
effort then turned into measured and rewarded spectacle
our bodies keep the imprint of a use that is no longer needed
text: In the beginning, running was no pastime at all. It was a duty: you ran to chase down game, you ran to carry word, you ran to get away from something that meant you harm. Because staying alive rested on endurance, our forebears kept, without ever once choosing it, legs that could hold a modest pace across enormous stretches of ground. Out of that need came a strange sort of body, with a springy cord at the heel, skin that sweats freely, and a head held level by one thin band of tissue. Then the settlements sprawled, the roads opened, beasts carried the loads we used to carry ourselves, and the need drained away. Effort turned into show. We began to time it, to compare it, to hand out crowns for it. That shift explains an oddity: our flesh still remembers a use our lives no longer ask of it.

units: the pain in the side ends many outings
a muscular sheet separates the rib cage from the abdomen
that sheet drives the breathing of the lungs
short, hurried breathing keeps it from letting go completely
its lasting contraction hauls on its anchor points
the pain shows up mostly under the ribs on the right side
easing the pace and drawing out the exhale is the first remedy
pressing the sore spot while folding the chest forward slackens the anchors
a heavy meal before the effort makes the trouble more likely
text: A stitch in the side ends more outings than most runners will admit, and its workings are easier to grasp than they sound. Under the lungs sits a broad sheet of muscle that walls the rib cage off from the belly, and that sheet is what pumps the air in and out. When breathing turns short and hurried, the sheet never fully lets go. It stays clenched and starts hauling on the places where it attaches. That is when the ache arrives, low under the ribs, usually on the right. Three fixes cover almost every case. First, ease the pace and drag out each exhale, blowing steadily as the foot opposite the ache lands. Second, press a hand into the sore spot and fold the chest forward, which slackens the attachments. Third, skip the big meal beforehand, since a full stomach shoves the sheet upward.

units: the athlete interviewed now plays in goal
she began her career in an attacking position
it took her seasons to see how opposed the two roles are
the forward moves toward open ground
the forward must drop her misses at once
the keeper falls back toward her own line
the keeper must hold on to every detail, since her lapses are paid for on the spot
in her first match in goal, she turned aside a low shot
the crowd rose to its feet after that save
she holds that both positions ask for equal courage
text: A goalkeeper once shared a memory with me that lays her trade bare. She had come up through the ranks as a forward, and it took her several seasons to see that the two positions obey opposite laws. A forward, she explained, moves toward open ground: she has to break at the right instant, slip past a defender, and drop every miss the moment it happens. A keeper does the reverse. She retreats toward her own line and has to hold on to every last detail, because a lapse there is paid for on the spot. On the evening of her first match in goal, she threw herself at a low shot and turned it away with her wrist. The whole crowd came to its feet. She understood something she had never felt as a forward: a team thanking her for an act of defense. Both roles, she now insists, ask for the same courage.

units: getting a session ready runs through four parts in order
the first part covers the gear and its condition
a rubbing seam or careless lacing brings on a skin injury
the second part is waking the body up
it combines brisk walking, joint circles, and short bursts of speed
the third part alternates quick stretches and easy ones
the pace chosen must stay bearable without tightening the breathing
the fourth part is winding down, drinking, and lengthening the legs
noting the tiredness felt in a notebook records the progress
text: Build your session in four parts, and keep them in this order. Part one is your gear. Check the laces, check that the sole is holding, and run a finger along the seams, because a blister starts with one rough edge that nobody bothered to look at. Part two wakes the body up. Walk briskly, roll the joints of the legs through their range, then finish off with a few short bursts of speed before the real start. Part three is the body of the session. Trade quick stretches for easy ones, holding a pace you can carry without your breathing going tight. Part four brings you back down. Slow in stages, drink, then lengthen the muscles of the thigh and the calf with no jerking. Last, note in a notebook how tired you felt. Week by week, that record tells you whether you are truly improving.

units: rain was falling when the first competitor reached the platform
people feared the event would be called off
the wind dropping left the water perfectly still
the organizers then sent off the first heats
the opening diver entered the water with almost no splash
the strictest judge handed her a high mark
a competitor slipped on the wet board and chose to withdraw
the setup was wiped dry before the restart
the defending champion pulled off a figure never tried at this site
she finished ahead of every one of her rivals
text: Rain was already coming down when the first competitor climbed up to the platform, and honestly, half of us figured the whole thing would be scrapped. It was not. The wind died off, the surface went perfectly still, and the organizers sent off the opening heats. That first dive shut everyone up: she slid in with barely a splash, and the judge nobody can please handed her a high mark. Then it got messy. One competitor slipped on the soaked board, caught himself at the last second, and decided he was done for the day. Crews wiped everything dry and the diving picked up again. Late on, the defending champion went for a figure nobody had ever tried at this pool, a tucked reversal, and she landed it clean. Climbing out, still laughing, she had beaten every rival in the field.

units: a smell of resin and chalk meets the visitor at the door
the climbing wall runs the full height of the building
the colored holds trace routes that are hard to read
thick mats cover the floor and swallow the noise of falls
all you hear is rubber squeaking and the breathing of the climbers
the openings stay shut to keep fingers from going cold
keeping them shut makes the heat build in the room
a teenage girl hesitates, then throws herself at a distant hold
her foot skids and the rope stops her halfway up
repeating the attempts is what brings the progress
text: The smell reaches you right at the door: resin, and the dry chalk that everyone carries on their hands. The climbing wall runs the full height of the building, and its colored holds trace paths the eye follows without ever making sense of them. Because thick mats swallow the floor, a fall lands without a sound. All you hear is rubber squeaking on stone and the breathing of the climbers overhead. The room grows warm, since every opening stays shut against the drafts that turn fingers stiff and useless. At the base of the wall a teenage girl hesitates, then throws herself at a hold well out of reach. Her foot skids, the swing spins her sideways, and the rope stops her halfway up. She lowers off, blows on her palms, starts over. Those attempts repeat, and that is where progress comes from.

units: the writer finds it wrong to file movement away among amusements
children now spend their afternoons seated in front of a screen
that stillness harms the skeleton, the eyesight, and the sleep
blaming families is convenient and unfair
the streets have closed to play
school yards have shrunk
the adult timetable no longer leaves a free gap
the writer calls for places where noise and falling are tolerated
he proposes opening the covered yards outside teaching hours
he argues that physical tiredness is the mark of an active life
text: We filed movement away under amusements, and the bill for that decision has come due. The child who used to climb, to jump, to roll down a grassy bank now spends the whole afternoon seated, a screen within reach. His bones show it, his eyes show it, his sleep shows it worst of all. Blaming parents is easy and unfair. The street shut its doors to play, the school yards were shaved down, and the adult timetable no longer leaves a single loose hour. Getting out of this costs no great budget and calls for no untried doctrine. Give children back places where noise is allowed and falling is expected. Open the covered yards outside teaching hours. Accept that a walk on foot is worth more than a parking spot saved. And stop treating a tired body as an accident: it is the mark of a life being used.
